# Interviewer guide — Question 4: sync job delete semantics

Interviewer-facing. Don't share this file or its contents with the
candidate.

## Source note

This is drawn from a real production bug in Berkeleytime's course puller
(`apps/datapuller/src/lib/api/sis-api.ts` and
`apps/datapuller/src/pullers/courses.ts`, fixed in commit `06dd8d6c8`). Two
related bugs, in the same sync job:

1. The puller fetched ACTIVE/FUTURE courses from SIS and deleted every
   *stored* course whose `courseId` was absent from that fetch. The store
   holds one row per `(courseId, subject, number)` because courses get
   renumbered and past-term classes still join against the old numbers; the
   fetch is deduped to current numbers only. So the delete logic targeted
   all 42,304 discontinued courses, over 10,000 of which were still
   referenced by past-term classes.

   There was a "ratio guard" in front of it: abort if the fetch came back
   under 95% of `countDocuments()`. Because of the modeling mismatch above,
   the ratio was structurally stuck around 28% — so **the guard fired on
   every single run, silently, for months.** No course created since then
   had ever landed in the database. Nobody noticed until someone went
   looking for a specific missing course. This is worth dwelling on in the
   debrief: the bug wasn't just wrong delete logic, it was wrong delete
   logic wrapped in a safety check that made the failure *quieter* rather
   than *safer* — the job kept reporting success while doing nothing.

2. Separately, page fetches from SIS were allowed to fail up to a 10%
   threshold per batch, with failures silently treated as empty results.
   SIS paginates by courseId, and a single course's rows can straddle a
   page boundary (verified live: courseId 160634 spanned pages 1900 and
   1901). Losing one of those pages can make the fetch look like it's
   missing one `(courseId, subject, number)` key for a course when really
   that data just failed to load — which the delete-superseded-rows logic
   would then read as "this row is stale" and delete.

The real fix: delete only rows whose `courseId` is in the fetch but whose
specific `(courseId, subject, number)` is not (i.e., superseded numbers
only — never infer deletion from a courseId's total absence). And: treat
404 as genuine end-of-data, but any other page failure that exhausts
retries aborts the whole write with a visible thrown error, rather than
being silently absorbed.

## Round 1 discussion guide

### Delete semantics — designs to listen for

1. **Delete only what's explicitly superseded/invalidated** (courseId
   present in the fetch, but this specific sub-key isn't). What BT
   converged on. Safe, cheap, requires the store's key granularity to
   actually distinguish "renumbered" from "discontinued" — candidate should
   notice that this only works because the key is finer than upstream's
   identity.
2. **Soft-delete / mark-stale-and-filter.** Never hard-delete; flag rows
   not seen in N consecutive fetches as inactive, filter them out
   downstream. Safer against flaky fetches, but pushes complexity onto
   every reader and needs a retention/cleanup policy eventually, or the
   store grows forever.
3. **Reference-counting before delete.** Check whether anything else in the
   local store points at an entity before removing it. Correct in spirit
   but couples the sync job to the schema of everything that might
   reference it, and silently breaks the moment a new referencing table is
   added and nobody updates the sync job. Worth asking: "what happens when
   you add a new table that joins on this six months from now?"
4. **Full replace-on-success, gated by a completeness guarantee** (checksum
   or count from the source). Ask why a ratio/threshold guard is a weak
   proxy for this — the real bug is a great counterexample: the ratio was
   *structurally* wrong (comparing deduped-by-number counts to
   one-row-per-number storage), so the guard didn't fail open when it
   should have fired, and didn't fail loud when it did fire. A guard based
   on a fuzzy heuristic threshold tends to either never fire or always
   fire; a good candidate should be suspicious of "abort if under X%" as a
   completeness signal at all.

None of these are "the" answer. Give credit for a candidate who picks one,
names what it costs, and can articulate when they'd switch to another.

### Fetch completeness — designs to listen for

1. **All-or-nothing:** any unretryable page failure aborts the whole write.
   What BT shipped. Simple, safe, but means a job with one flaky page does
   *zero* useful work that run, even for entities on other pages that
   fetched fine.
2. **Best-effort with visible staleness reporting:** write what succeeded,
   but flag which entities are now "possibly stale" and retry just those
   next run. More available, more code, and only as good as whatever
   consumes the "possibly stale" signal — ask what happens if nothing does.
3. **Two-phase — stage then validate then reconcile:** fetch everything
   into a staging area first, check completeness there, only reconcile
   against the live store if the staged fetch passes. Cleanly separates
   "did we get everything" from "what do we do about what we got," at the
   cost of needing somewhere to stage a full snapshot.

### Follow-ups

- "How would you have caught this bug in production before a user did?"
  Listen for: alerting on zero-write runs, alerting on delete counts past
  some sane bound, a metric on fetch completeness distinct from "job
  succeeded," a dashboard nobody set up because "the job reported success"
  was treated as sufficient signal. This is the observability instinct
  check — the real bug went undetected for months precisely because the
  guard's failure mode was silent (early return, no throw, no metric).
- "What's the blast radius if your delete logic is wrong in production for
  a week before anyone notices?" Good candidates distinguish between
  "wrongly deletes things" (recoverable if idempotent re-fetch restores
  them next run) and "wrongly fails to delete things" (stale data lingers,
  probably less harmful) and reason about which failure mode their design
  biases toward.

### Red flags

- Proposes "delete anything not in this fetch" and never questions what
  "absent from the fetch" could mean beyond "no longer exists upstream."
- No mention of partial/incomplete fetches at all, even after being asked
  directly about fetch reliability.
- Treats a threshold/ratio guard as sufficient completeness validation
  without being able to say what happens when the guard itself is
  miscalibrated (i.e., doesn't independently reason about the guard's own
  correctness).
- Can't articulate any downside to their chosen design when pushed.

## Round 2 code review guide

### What the tests check

The starter ships `reconcileCourses` as a stub (`throw new Error("not
implemented")`), so all four tests in `impl/test/reconcile.test.ts` fail
identically before the candidate writes anything. What matters is what each
one verifies about a *correct* implementation:

- **Normal reconciliation** — a row's title changes and must be upserted
  correctly, while an unrelated discontinued-but-referenced course (present
  in the store, absent from every fetch) must be left alone. This is the
  first check that the candidate didn't implement "delete anything whose
  courseId isn't in the fetch."
- **Renumbering** — store has a stale old-number row and an already-synced
  new-number row for the same courseId; the fetch reports only the new
  number. Correct behavior deletes the old-number row (the superseded
  sub-key) and keeps the new one, while still leaving the unrelated
  discontinued course untouched. This is the test that separates "deletes
  nothing" (fails here) from "deletes based on courseId absence" (fails
  the normal-reconciliation and discontinued-but-referenced tests instead).
  A correct implementation has to thread the needle: delete the specific
  superseded key, but never the courseId's other rows.
- **Discontinued-but-referenced** — isolates the same invariant (a course
  entirely absent from the fetch must survive) with a class record that
  depends on it, made explicit for readability.
- **Partial fetch** — `fetchCourses()` reports non-empty `failedPages`.
  Correct behavior throws rather than reconciling; nothing in the store
  should change.

### Reference solution shape

This is one correct approach — not the only one. It satisfies the contract
in the JSDoc above the stub and passes all four tests:

```ts
export async function reconcileCourses(
  input: ReconcileInput
): Promise<ReconcileResult> {
  const { stored, fetchCourses } = input;

  const { courses, failedPages } = await fetchCourses();

  if (failedPages.length > 0) {
    throw new Error(
      `Incomplete fetch: ${failedPages.length} page(s) failed: ${failedPages.join(", ")}`
    );
  }

  const fetchedCourseIds = new Set(courses.map((c) => c.courseId));
  const fetchedKeys = new Set(
    courses.map((c) => `${c.courseId}|${c.subject}|${c.number}`)
  );

  // Keep a stored row unless its courseId is in the fetch AND its specific
  // (courseId, subject, number) key is NOT -- i.e. delete only superseded
  // numbers, never a courseId's total absence.
  const nextStored: StoredCourseRow[] = stored.filter(
    (row) =>
      !fetchedCourseIds.has(row.courseId) ||
      fetchedKeys.has(`${row.courseId}|${row.subject}|${row.number}`)
  );
  const deletedCount = stored.length - nextStored.length;

  let upsertedCount = 0;
  for (const course of courses) {
    const idx = nextStored.findIndex(
      (row) =>
        row.courseId === course.courseId &&
        row.subject === course.subject &&
        row.number === course.number
    );

    if (idx >= 0) {
      nextStored[idx] = { ...course };
    } else {
      nextStored.push({ ...course });
    }
    upsertedCount += 1;
  }

  return { stored: nextStored, upsertedCount, deletedCount };
}
```

This has been verified locally against the test suite (all 4 pass with this
shape; all 4 fail against the stub, as expected).

Acceptable variations: throwing a custom error type instead of `Error`;
computing `fetchedKeys` with a tuple/array key instead of a string join;
restructuring into named helper functions; different upsert strategies
(e.g. a Map keyed by the composite key instead of `findIndex`). Not
acceptable: any version that still infers deletion from courseId absence,
or that still proceeds (even with a warning) when `failedPages` is
non-empty.

### AI-tool-usage questions

- "Did the AI's first draft handle both requirements — delete semantics
  and fetch completeness — or only one of the two?" A plausible
  wrong-but-tempting AI output: implementing fetch-completeness correctly
  (throwing on `failedPages`) while still deleting on courseId-absence, or
  vice versa, since the two requirements are easy to reason about (and
  implement) independently, and a model asked to "implement this function"
  might satisfy whichever requirement it locks onto first and treat the
  other as already handled. Ask whether the candidate caught this
  themselves by rereading the contract, or whether the tests caught it for
  them.
- "Did you ask the tool to explain why `(courseId, subject, number)` is the
  right key before or after it wrote code?" — probing whether they
  understood the domain modeling before or only after the fact.
- Ask them to explain, without looking at code, why "absent from the
  fetch" isn't a safe deletion signal. If they can only explain it by
  pointing at the code the AI wrote, that's a gap.

### Red flags

- Passes the happy-path test but the implementation doesn't generalize —
  e.g. hardcodes behavior around the specific fixture courseIds/titles
  rather than the general key comparison.
- Implementation satisfies only one of the two requirements (delete
  semantics or fetch completeness), and the candidate doesn't notice until
  pointed at the failing test.
- Edited the test file or fixtures to make tests pass instead of fixing
  `reconcile.ts`.
- Cannot explain, when asked directly, why a courseId being absent from a
  fetch doesn't imply every row for it should be deleted.
- No partial-fetch handling at all, or handling that swallows the error
  instead of surfacing it (e.g. catches and logs instead of throwing).

## Rubric (1-5 each)

| Dimension | 1 | 3 | 5 |
|---|---|---|---|
| System design judgment | Proposes delete-on-absence with no caveats; no completeness handling | Names one reasonable design per sub-problem, some tradeoff awareness | Names multiple designs per sub-problem, picks one, explains exactly what it costs and when they'd switch |
| Code quality / correctness | Implementation doesn't generalize past the fixtures, or only satisfies one of the two requirements | Implementation is correct and passes tests, some rough edges (weak naming, no comments) | Implementation is correct, general, readable, and the candidate can defend every line |
| Tradeoff articulation | Can't name a downside to their own design when pushed | Names a downside when asked | Volunteers downsides unprompted, ties them to concrete failure scenarios |
| AI-tool usage judgment | Accepted AI output without checking it against the domain; can't explain the implementation without the code in front of them | Reviewed AI output, caught at least one issue | Drove the tool with the domain constraints up front, caught subtle AI mistakes (e.g. satisfying only one of the two requirements), can explain every line independent of the tool |
| Communication | Vague, can't walk through their own reasoning when asked | Clear explanation when prompted | Proactively narrates tradeoffs and reasoning without prompting |

## Time budget

This question has more moving parts *conceptually* than most in the kit —
two interacting requirements and a non-trivial domain model — even though
the resulting implementation is small (well under 30 lines, one file, no
external dependencies). Round 1 can reasonably run
to the full 60 minutes if the candidate engages with the interaction
between the two sub-problems (most candidates will need the prompting
follow-up to get there). For Round 2, don't be alarmed if a strong
candidate using AI tools well converges on a correct diff well inside an
hour — that's the right outcome, not a sign the exercise was too easy.
Fast completion isn't suspicious here; use the remaining time for the
edge-case probes and AI-usage questions below rather than expecting the
coding itself to fill 3-4 hours.
